documents.title: Policies and Guidance: Generative AI
documents.summary: IU system-wide teaching page saying IU has no AI-specific policy beyond data security, naming Copilot as preferred tool, and pointing to existing misconduct rules. It offers two sample syllabus statements (open and strict) and advice from an IU Bloomington professor on communicating and framing AI policy.
documents.stance_why: The page states "IU does not currently have any specific policies around the use of generative AI" and offers a "Least restrictive" and "Most restrictive" syllabus example "that you may consider as starting templates", so the decision is left to instructors with tiers as templates; stance is delegates.

units.why: The page says "IU does not currently have any specific policies around the use of generative AI" apart from data rules, which leaves AI decisions to instructors; P04 fits better than P56 because no framework is stated. It is a fact about the institution addressed to all.
units.anchor: IU does not currently have any specific policies around the use of generative AI

units.why: "Microsoft Copilot ... is IU's preferred generative AI service for faculty and staff" recommends a vetted tool; P50 (prefer vetted tools) fits better than P17 because it is a preference tied to data level, not a course tool.
units.anchor: is IU's preferred generative AI service for faculty and staff

units.why: "When using public tools, usage of data is more restrictive, even when the data are anonymized" sets a data limit on public AI tools; P50 protects data.
units.anchor: usage of data is more restrictive, even when the data are anonymized
units.frag_end: even when the data are anonymized.

units.why: IU "provides a Data Classification Matrix to help faculty make the most appropriate decisions with using data" is guidance on protecting data when using AI, so P50 (protect data).
units.anchor: Data Classification Matrix
units.policy: IU provides a Data Classification Matrix to help faculty make the most appropriate decisions with using data.

units.why: "Students are expected to adhere to the Code of Student Rights, Responsibilities, and Conduct, which addresses Academic Misconduct" ties AI use to existing misconduct rules; P36 fits.
units.anchor: Students are expected to adhere to the Code of

units.why: "it may be useful for instructors to address generative AI more specifically, such as in their syllabi" recommends syllabus statements; P09 (state expectations in syllabus), weak modality (should) because it says "may be useful".
units.anchor: it may be useful for instructors to address generative AI more specifically

units.why: The page offers "sample syllabus statements that you may consider as starting templates", a least and most restrictive example; this is a set of named levels, so P05 rather than P04 (tiers are explicit).
units.anchor: sample syllabus statements that you may consider as starting templates

units.why: The least restrictive example says "generative AI (GAI) is permitted in this course for all assignments and assessments with no penalty", an open default; P02 permit by default.
units.anchor: is permitted in this course for all assignments and assessments with no penalty

units.why: "all large language models ... still have a large tendency to make up incorrect facts or fake citations" warns that outputs are unreliable; P31 (verify; often wrong).
units.anchor: still have a large tendency to make up incorrect facts or fake citations

units.why: "You will be responsible for any inaccurate, biased, offensive, or otherwise unethical content you submit regardless of whether it originally comes from you or a GAI platform" makes students owners of submissions; P29.
units.anchor: You will be responsible for any inaccurate, biased, offensive, or otherwise unethical content

units.why: "Any use of such tools must be appropriately acknowledged and cited" is a disclosure duty with each submission; P24.
units.anchor: Any use of such tools must be appropriately acknowledged and cited.

units.why: "The disclosure of use of GAI for spelling and grammar checkers is not necessary" exempts a use from disclosure. I chose P24 (disclosure scope) over P18 (prose vs code) because the rule is about what must be disclosed.
units.anchor: The disclosure of use of GAI for spelling and grammar checkers is not necessary
units.policy: The disclosure of use of GAI for spelling and grammar checkers is not necessary, but all other uses of GAI require proper acknowledgment and citations.

units.why: "Use of GAI without acknowledgement will result in a penalty" makes non-disclosure the violation; P28.
units.anchor: Use of GAI without acknowledgement will result in a penalty.

units.why: The APA example "OpenAI. (2024). ChatGPT (Mar 14 version) [Large language model]." shows citing the tool, version and date; P25.
units.anchor: OpenAI. (2024). ChatGPT (Mar 14 version) [Large language model].
units.policy: Cite generative AI in APA style, naming the developer, year, tool, version and the model type, as in the example given.

units.why: "The use of GAI platforms without disclosure will be considered plagiarism and/or cheating and will be reported to the Dean of Students" classes undisclosed use as misconduct; P36.
units.anchor: considered plagiarism and/or cheating and will be reported to the Dean of Students

units.why: "Sanctions ... may include a failing grade on the assignment, a reduction in your final course grade, or a failing grade in the course" states concrete penalties; P37.
units.anchor: a failing grade on the assignment, a reduction in your final course

units.why: "please consult with the instructor before submitting your work" tells unsure students to ask first; P10.
units.anchor: please consult with the instructor before submitting your work.

units.why: "we encourage the use of GAI as a means for you to submit higher quality" welcomes use; P02.
units.anchor: we encourage the use of GAI as a means for you to submit higher quality

units.why: "Learning how to use Gen AI is an emerging skill, and it would be to your advantage to learn how to use it well" gives a professional-skill rationale; P44.
units.anchor: Learning how to use Gen AI is an emerging skill
units.frag_end: learn how to use it well.

units.why: "it is not a replacement for critical thinking" says AI must not replace the student's thinking; P32.
units.anchor: it is not a replacement for critical thinking.

units.why: The most restrictive example says GAI tools "is strictly prohibited for any part of your assignments", a full ban by default; P01.
units.anchor: is strictly prohibited for any part of your assignments
units.frag_start: The use of generative AI (GAI) tools, such as

units.why: The list "chatbots, text generators, paraphrasers, summarizers, or solvers" defines which tools the restrictive statement covers; P61 (define scope).
units.anchor: chatbots, text generators, paraphrasers, summarizers, or solvers
units.frag_start: The use of generative AI (GAI) tools, such as
units.policy: The restrictive statement covers GAI tools such as chatbots, text generators, paraphrasers, summarizers, or solvers.

units.why: "Students must complete all work independently and without GAI-generated content" bars submitting AI-generated work; P19 rather than P01 because it is about content submitted as one's own.
units.anchor: Students must complete all work independently and without GAI-generated content.

units.why: "you are expected to do your own work and properly cite any sources you use" makes the student owner of the work; P29.
units.anchor: you are expected to do your own work and properly cite any sources you use
units.frag_start: In this course, you are expected

units.why: "you should always check with your department, school, or campus to see if there are specific GenAI statements or policies" sends instructors to lower-level rules; P04 (decision sits with the unit) rather than P09.
units.anchor: always check with your department, school, or campus
units.frag_start: Of course, you should always check
units.policy: You should always check with your department, school, or campus to see if there are specific GenAI statements or policies that should be included.

units.why: The suggested disclaimer says AI tools "should not be used for any work for this class without explicit permission of the instructor and appropriate attribution", a silent-means-no rule; P06.
units.anchor: should not be used for any work for this class without explicit permission

units.why: "Include the policy on your syllabus" is the first of several steps for communicating the policy; P09.
units.anchor: Include the policy on your syllabus
units.policy: Include the AI policy on your syllabus.

units.why: "Remind students of the policy for each relevant assignment" asks for per-assignment restatement; P09 (communicate expectations) fits, P11 does not because it is about repeating, not scoping.
units.anchor: Remind students of the policy for each relevant assignment
units.policy: Remind students of the AI policy for each relevant assignment by including it, in some form, on assignment handouts/guides and Canvas pages.

units.why: "Students have multiple classes, each which may have some variation in generative AI policy" explains that rules differ across courses; P11.
units.anchor: each which may have some variation in generative AI policy

units.why: "students need to learn how to use these tools and to do so responsibly" is a professional-skills rationale; P44.
units.anchor: students need to learn how to use these tools and to do so responsibly

units.why: "Banning them outright is not only likely a losing battle, but may do students a disservice" argues against bans and "leaning into the possibilities" is recommended; P02 (permit/encourage by default) fits better than P03.
units.anchor: leaning into the possibilities and helping students learn to ethically and responsibly use these technologies
units.policy: Instead of banning AI outright, lean into the possibilities and help students learn to ethically and responsibly use these technologies.

units.why: "There are some clear cases where banning these tools make sense (e.g., language acquisition courses)" lets some courses ban AI; P04 since the choice is per course.
units.anchor: There are some clear cases where banning these tools make sense

documents.unit: Center for Teaching and Learning, IU Indianapolis
documents.title: Generative AI in the Classroom FAQs
documents.summary: Campus teaching-center FAQ for faculty. It reports Copilot as the only approved tool for internal data, advises against detectors, and recommends a learner-centered, non-punitive approach. It sets no student rule and leaves syllabus policy to instructors and departments.
documents.stance_why: The FAQ sets no course-level rule on AI use; it says to "check with your department to ensure your syllabus policy aligns" and recommends approaches ("proactive rather than punitive"), so decisions are left to instructors; stance is delegates.

units.why: "Indiana University has approved the use of Microsoft Copilot for faculty, staff, and students aged 18 and older" names a sanctioned tool; P17 fits better than P50 because the unit is approval of a tool.
units.anchor: approved the use of Microsoft Copilot for faculty, staff, and students aged 18 and older.

units.why: "This is the only generative AI tool approved for use that involves university internal data" limits which tool may handle internal data; P50 (vetted tools).
units.anchor: the only generative AI tool approved for use that involves university internal data
units.frag_start: This is the only generative AI tool approved

units.why: "IU has also established an AI Taskforce that has developed AI recommendations" describes an institution-level body producing guidance; P56 (framework).
units.anchor: IU has also established an AI Taskforce that has developed AI recommendations.

units.why: "We recommend adopting a learner-centered approach when talking with students about their use of AI" asks instructors to talk before escalating; P57.
units.anchor: We recommend adopting a learner-centered approach when talking with students about their use of AI.

units.why: Instructors can use AI "from creating rubrics and course learning objectives" to making content relevant; P59 (instructor AI use for teaching work).
units.anchor: creating rubrics and course learning objectives
units.frag_start: There are many ways that you as
units.policy: Instructors may use AI tools to help generate content for research and teaching, from creating rubrics and course learning objectives to making content more relevant to their students.

units.why: "make sure to consider IU's Acceptable Uses of Generative AI" tells instructors to follow the data-use rules when using AI; P50.
units.anchor: make sure to consider IU’s Acceptable Uses of Generative AI

units.why: "IU has not approved any IU detection tools for use" says no detector is sanctioned; P39 (do not rely on detectors).
units.anchor: IU has not approved any IU detection tools for use
units.policy: IU has not approved any detection tools for use.

units.why: "AI detection tools are unreliable, which can cause students to be falsely accused of academic misconduct" gives the reason detectors should not be relied on; P39.
units.anchor: AI detection tools are unreliable

units.why: "AI detection software targets specific demographics, especially non-native English writers" names a bias harm of detectors; P53 (bias and harms) chosen over P39, which is about reliability.
units.anchor: AI detection software targets specific demographics, especially non-native English writers

units.why: "It is essential to ensure that students use AI tools to help develop and hone critical thinking skills as opposed to circumvent learning" asks that AI not replace student thinking; P32.
units.anchor: AI tools to help develop and hone critical thinking skills as opposed to circumvent learning

units.why: Instructors should check the department so the syllabus policy aligns with it ("ensure your syllabus policy aligns with any policies and/or recommendations your department may have"); P04 fits (unit-level rules).
units.anchor: ensure your syllabus policy aligns with any policies and/or recommendations your department may have
units.frag_start: It is important to check with your department

units.why: "early research indicates AI has not increased cheating" cites evidence on AI and integrity; P55.
units.anchor: early research indicates AI has not increased cheating
units.frag_start: It may surprise you to learn that

units.why: "We recommend faculty adopt a proactive rather than punitive approach to the use of AI" gives a stance on handling AI that fits no listed type (P57 is about talking before escalating, P35 about redesign).
units.anchor: adopt a proactive rather than punitive approach to the use of AI
units.uncovered_note: Faculty should take a proactive rather than punitive approach to student AI use.

units.why: "Students who understand the purpose of their assignments and are invested in their own learning are less likely to over rely on AI tools" suggests clarifying assignment purpose to reduce over-reliance; no type covers it.
units.anchor: Students who understand the purpose of their assignments
units.uncovered_note: Explaining assignment purposes and building student investment reduces over-reliance on AI.

units.why: "instructors cannot require that students use AI tools" because Copilot is not available to all; P51 (no required tools, equity).
units.anchor: instructors cannot require that students use AI tools
units.frag_start: Because this tool is not available to all students,

units.why: "Always advise students to exercise caution and consider the data privacy risks associated with generative AI use" asks instructors to warn about data; P50.
units.anchor: Always advise students to exercise caution and consider the data privacy risks

units.why: "make sure to have a disclaimer regarding privacy" applies when an instructor chooses to use AI in a class; P50.
units.anchor: make sure to have a disclaimer regarding privacy
units.frag_start: Should you choose to use AI in your class,
units.policy: If you choose to use AI in your class, include a disclaimer regarding privacy.

units.why: "ensure there are alternative ways for students to engage" requires alternatives; P51.
units.anchor: ensure there are alternative ways for students to engage
units.frag_start: Should you choose to use AI in your class,
units.policy: If you use AI in your class, ensure there are alternative ways for students to engage should they not wish to use AI.

units.why: "there are inherent biases within the algorithms as well as biases within the data" names bias concerns; P53.
units.anchor: there are inherent biases
units.frag_start: While AI tools cannot have intentional biases
units.policy: AI tools have inherent biases within the algorithms and within the data on which models are trained.

units.why: "It is imperative to verify AI outputs and always consider the limitations of these tools" requires checking AI output; P31.
units.anchor: verify AI outputs and always consider the limitations of these tools

units.why: "Make sure to read user agreements before using AI tools" ties to IP and terms of use; P52 (terms of use) rather than P50 because it concerns agreements.
units.anchor: Make sure to read user agreements before using AI tools

notes: Two university-layer documents only; no school/computing documents found. Several teachiu units cite IU Bloomington sample statements and advice (templates, not IU policy). Two UNCOVERED units in the CTL FAQ (proactive-not-punitive approach; clarifying assignment purpose).
